site_description: An opinionated TanStack Start starter with enforced boundaries, typed data, authentication, and a complete vertical example.
home_title_second: for apps that never stay simple.¹
home_description: The thing nobody tells you about web applications, back when everything is still greenfield and pure possibility, is that every single one of them eventually has to decide who owns which piece of state, who is allowed to talk to the database, and what happens to the data when the schema changes; and that you will make these decisions either now, calmly, with tests, or later, at approximately 2 a.m., without them.² This starter makes them now.
home_features_eyebrow: What is actually in the box
home_features_title: A working application, including the parts you were going to do later.
home_features_description: Everything below is wired together and shown working in one small notes feature, on the theory that a starter which merely lists auth, data, email, localization, logging, CI, and deployment as things you could plausibly add yourself has not really started anything.³
home_feature_1_description: TanStack Start SSR, file routing, loader prefetching, Query hydration, and route-level loading, error, and not-found states. The last three are the ones everyone means to do properly and then ships without.
home_feature_2_description: Better Auth magic links, PostgreSQL sessions, rate limits, optional Google and GitHub OAuth, React Email templates, and Resend in production. Locally the magic link prints to your terminal, so trying any of it needs no real inbox.
home_feature_3_description: Owner-scoped summaries and detail reads, private and unlisted access, public read-only links, soft deletion, a validated editor, autosave, local drafts, undo/redo. One feature taken through every layer, which is the only way to see what a real one costs.
home_feature_4_description: Typed domain operations, reviewed Drizzle migrations for relational changes, version-stamped JSONB where a payload can change incompatibly, seeds, and exactly one named owner for every piece of state (Query, form, URL, or store), settled before the argument starts.
home_feature_5_description: English and German localized URLs, SSR-safe locale handling, localized MDX with fallbacks, sitemap and robots routes, optional PostHog events. The second language is mostly there as proof that the first one was never hardcoded.
home_feature_6_description: Tailwind design tokens with light and dark palettes, slimmed shadcn-derived Radix primitives, cva variants, accessible forms, reduced-motion support. Semantic tokens throughout, so dark mode stays one decision instead of forty small corrections.
home_feature_7_description: CSRF protection, per-operation authorization, validated environments, security headers, sanitized errors, structured logs, correlation IDs, health checks. Nobody looks at any of it until the one morning it is missing.
home_feature_8_description: Repository guidance, area-specific skills, feature runbooks, architecture lint rules, strict types, tests, and guardrails on generated files, so a coding agent inherits this architecture instead of confidently inventing a worse one.
home_feature_9_description: GitHub Actions with drift checks, a non-root precompressed container, graceful shutdown, exact-commit Railway releases, and an optional HMAC-authenticated FastAPI service for the parts of the problem that insist on being Python.
home_principles_title: Six decisions taken in advance, on purpose, so nothing decides them for you later.
home_principle_1_description: Dependencies point one way: components to hooks, hooks to queries, queries to server functions, and only server code at the database. Every server function validates its input and checks ownership right where the data is touched, because a redirect in the route is a courtesy to the user and no obstacle at all to anyone with the network tab open. Lint rules and build checks enforce the direction; a convention that lives only in a document is enforced by nothing.
home_principle_2_description: Strict TypeScript from the database to the UI: models derived from the schema itself, branded IDs, one source per enum. Untrusted values are parsed exactly once, at the place where they enter, and are plain typed data afterward. Assertions outside tests are rejected by a custom lint rule, since an assertion is just a promise about a value, and the runtime has never once read your promises.
home_principle_3_description: TanStack Query owns remote records and their cache, the URL owns shareable filters, React Hook Form owns field interaction, scoped Zustand stores own drafts and undo history, and PostgreSQL owns durable data. One owner each, which sounds too obvious to write down until you have debugged the same value in three places at once. Loaders and components share the same query definitions, every write goes through a domain hook, and an active draft is never overwritten by a cache refresh that arrived mid-sentence.
home_principle_4_description: Environment configuration is validated at boot, so a missing variable stops the process instead of producing a subtly wrong Tuesday, and CSRF protection is installed explicitly, not inherited by luck. Expected failures return stable machine codes, unexpected ones return a generic message, and the actual cause goes to the logs, structured and redacted and under a correlation ID, where it is useful to you and to nobody else.
home_principle_5_description: Relational changes go through reviewed SQL migrations. Stored JSONB carries a compatibility version only where an aggregate needs one, browser drafts carry a version of their own, and incompatible payload changes move through resumable backfills you can dry-run first. All of it is more ceremony than it looks worth, right up until the one afternoon it is worth every minute.
home_principle_6_description: Thirteen area skills encode the architecture as working contracts. One loads whenever work enters its area and walks a human or a coding agent through the runbook, a new domain or a new store, so the pattern gets read at the moment of use and not remembered approximately. Lint rules, write guards, and CI drift checks backstop whatever a contract cannot enforce by itself.⁴
home_setup_title: Getting to localhost is the boring part, which is the point.
home_setup_description: You copy one environment file (two required variables, both documented), run the five commands in order, and arrive at a database, a dev server, and a working notes app, without once being asked to have a transformative personal experience with a YAML file.⁵
home_setup_node_requirement: Node and pnpm, at the versions the repository already pins for you
home_setup_docker_requirement: Docker, for the PostgreSQL database that comes with it
home_setup_python_requirement: Python and uv, only if you want the optional FastAPI service
home_setup_commands:
pnpm install
cp .env.example .env
pnpm docker:up
pnpm db:migrate
pnpm dev
home_footnote_1: “Supposedly simple” here meaning: TanStack Start, React, TanStack Query, Better Auth, Drizzle, PostgreSQL, Zod, Zustand, Tailwind, Paraglide, React Email, and Pino, pre-wired, with CI and Railway delivery attached, plus an optional FastAPI service for when one language is somehow not enough.
home_footnote_2: Q.v. the included notes feature (authentication, ownership, sharing, undo/redo, autosave, localization, tests), which exists precisely so that the phrase “left as an exercise for the reader” appears nowhere in this repository.
home_footnote_3: One feature carried all the way through is the only honest unit of measurement available here, it being easy to ship nine impressive-sounding integrations that have never once been asked to work at the same time, in the same request, for the same real user.
home_footnote_4: Enforced by lint rules and build-time guards rather than by the honor system, the honor system’s record in production software being what it is.
home_footnote_5: This entire page also exists in German, at a localized URL, with SSR-safe locale handling: the kind of detail nobody misses until approximately one hour before launch.
